result:
The soft hum of rain against the window always pulls me into a strange, delicious melancholy. There's something about water falling from the sky that reminds us we're still animals—creatures who once huddled in caves listening to the same rhythm, wondering if the storm would ever end or if the world was ending instead.

I’ve been thinking lately about how we’re all just walking libraries of forgotten things. Every person you pass carries entire civilizations in their bones: the way their grandmother laughed, the smell of their father’s workshop, the first time they tasted snow. We inherit these invisible inheritances and rarely speak of them. Instead we talk about traffic and what we had for lunch.

There’s a particular kind of freedom in writing without purpose. No audience to impress, no thesis to defend. Just the pure pleasure of stringing words together like a child might arrange seashells on the shore—because the arrangement feels right, because the colors complement each other, because why not?

The older I get, the more I suspect that meaning isn't something we discover but something we dare to create in the face of cosmic indifference. We plant gardens knowing winter will kill them. We fall in love knowing hearts break. We write messages in bottles and throw them into oceans we’ll never cross.

And yet.

The rain keeps falling. The words keep coming. And for this brief moment, that feels like enough. 

(248 words)
